title: Jesus Said He Would Spit Them Out—And the Most Terrifying Part Is They Thought They Were Fine
paragraphs: Jesus Said He Would Spit Them Out—And the Most Terrifying Part Is They Thought They Were Fine
The warning hidden inside “Do not be lukewarm” is more frightening—and more merciful—than many Christians realize.
There is a kind of spiritual danger that does not feel dangerous.
That may be what makes it so deadly.
You can still go to church.
Still know the worship songs.
Still post Bible verses.
Still say, “God is good.”
Still call yourself a Christian.
Still know exactly how to sound spiritual when someone asks how your walk with God is going.
And yet somewhere behind the Christian language, the Sunday routine, the worship playlist, the cross around your neck, and the Bible sitting beside your bed, something has quietly happened.
Jesus has moved from the center to the edges.
You have not necessarily denied Him.
You have simply learned how to live without desperately needing Him.
And one of the most frightening warnings Jesus ever gave was spoken to people who apparently did not realize anything was wrong.
Listen carefully to His words to the church in Laodicea:
“I know your deeds, that you are neither cold nor hot... because you are lukewarm—neither hot nor cold—I am about to spit you out of my mouth.” — Revelation 3:15–16
The New Testament was written in Greek, and the word translated “lukewarm” here is χλιαρός — chliaros.
Lukewarm.
Tepid.
Neither one thing nor the other.
And the verb Jesus uses for what He will do with that condition is equally disturbing: ἐμέσαι — emesai, from emeō.
To vomit.
To spit out.
This is not the vocabulary of mild disappointment.
Jesus is exposing something He finds intolerable.
But before we turn this passage into another angry sermon about Christians who “aren't on fire enough,” we need to notice something crucial.
The deepest problem in Laodicea was not merely a shortage of religious enthusiasm.
It was self-sufficiency.
Jesus tells us exactly what was wrong.
“You say, ‘I am rich; I have acquired wealth and do not need a thing.’”
Then He exposes the reality they cannot see:
“But you do not realize that you are wretched, pitiful, poor, blind and naked.” — Revelation 3:17
Read those words again.
“I do not need a thing.”
That is the heartbeat of lukewarm Christianity.
Not necessarily atheism.
Not always open rebellion.
Sometimes it is something far more respectable.
Jesus without dependence.
Christianity without surrender.
Prayer without desperation.
Worship without obedience.
Bible knowledge without repentance.
A cross displayed publicly while self still occupies the throne privately.
It is possible to have enough Christianity to feel religious while maintaining enough control to remain your own lord.
And that is why this passage should make every one of us uncomfortable before it ever makes us think about somebody else.
Because the easiest person to diagnose as lukewarm is someone else.
The hardest person is the one in the mirror.
Maybe you remember when conviction used to bother you.
You would sin, and something inside you would ache.
You would run back to God.
You would pray.
You would confess.
You wanted to be clean.
Then somewhere along the road, compromise became familiar.
What once terrified you became manageable.
What once made you repent became something you explained away.
The secret messages.
The hidden pornography.
The bitterness you keep feeding.
The relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
The money you would never surrender.
The unforgiveness you have renamed “boundaries” even though, deep inside, you know hatred has taken root.
The pride disguised as discernment.
The gossip disguised as concern.
The jealousy hidden beneath silence.
The secret life nobody at church knows exists.
Or maybe there is no spectacular scandal at all.
Maybe that is precisely the problem.
You simply stopped caring.
Your Bible remained closed a little longer.
Prayer became shorter.
Conviction became quieter.
Entertainment became easier to consume than Scripture.
Hours disappeared into scrolling while ten minutes with God felt exhausting.
You still believed in Jesus.
You just stopped living as though knowing Him was the greatest treasure you possessed.
And slowly...
almost invisibly...
Jesus became someone you included rather than Someone you followed.
That is why Laodicea is so frightening.
They were spiritually dying while believing they were doing well.
“I am rich.”
“I have prospered.”
“I need nothing.”
Jesus says, in effect:
You cannot even see what has happened to you.
There is a blindness worse than not knowing.
It is believing you can already see.
There is poverty worse than having nothing.
It is having everything except Christ and thinking you are rich.
There is nakedness worse than having no clothes.
It is standing spiritually exposed before God while convincing yourself that your religious reputation has covered you.
But then the passage does something astonishing.
Jesus does not simply condemn them.
He offers Himself.
He tells them to receive from Him the true riches they lack: gold refined by fire, white garments for their shame, and salve so their blind eyes can finally see.
Do you see the Gospel hiding inside the warning?
Their answer was not to manufacture enough spiritual passion to impress Jesus.
Their answer was to come back to Jesus.
The poor need what He possesses.
The naked need what He provides.
The blind need the sight He gives.
The self-sufficient must finally admit:
I need You.
And perhaps that is the sentence some of us have been avoiding.
Jesus, I need You.
Not merely when the diagnosis comes.
Not merely when the marriage collapses.
Not merely when the money disappears.
Not merely when someone dies.
Not merely when anxiety overwhelms me.
Not merely when every human solution has failed.
I need You when the bank account is full.
I need You when the family is healthy.
I need You when people applaud me.
I need You when ministry is growing.
I need You when life is comfortable.
I need You when nobody knows my secret.
I need You when I think I am doing fine.
Because prosperity can reveal something suffering often destroys:
the illusion that we can live without God.
And then comes one of the most important sentences in the entire warning.
Jesus says:
“Those whom I love I rebuke and discipline. So be earnest and repent.” — Revelation 3:19
There it is.
Love.
The warning is severe because the love is real.
Jesus is not exposing Laodicea because He delights in humiliating sinners.
He exposes them because He refuses to leave them comfortably dying.
The Greek language makes the urgency even sharper. Jesus tells them to be zealous and to repent—μετανόησον, metanoēson, from metanoeō: repent, change one's mind and direction.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling guilty.
It is not crying during worship and returning to the same rebellion Monday morning.
It is not posting a verse because conviction briefly hurt.
Repentance turns.
Repentance stops defending what Christ is confronting.
Repentance brings darkness into the light.
Repentance says, “Jesus, You are right about me.”
And grace says, “Come.”
That distinction matters because Christianity is not salvation by spiritual temperature.
We are not saved because we become passionate enough.
We are not justified because we pray loudly enough, cry deeply enough, evangelize frequently enough, or maintain flawless devotional routines.
We are saved by grace through faith, because of what Jesus Christ has accomplished—not because we successfully manufacture religious intensity.
The cross destroys boasting.
Christ carried sin.
Christ bore judgment.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ saves.
And genuine grace does not merely pardon us while leaving us comfortably enslaved. The Christ who forgives also calls us to follow Him.
So do not read Revelation 3 and hear:
“Try harder so Jesus will love you.”
Hear:
“Jesus loves enough to confront what is destroying you. Repent and return to Him.”
That is why the next image is breathtaking.
After the rebuke...
after the exposure...
after telling this church that it is poor, blind, naked, and nauseatingly lukewarm...
Jesus does not disappear.
He remains.
At the door.
Knocking.
“Here I am! I stand at the door and knock.” — Revelation 3:20
Think about that.
The One they pushed outside is still knocking.
The One they neglected is still speaking.
The One they treated as optional is still inviting them into fellowship.
That is grace.
Not sentimental grace that pretends sin does not matter.
Scandalous grace.
Holy grace.
Grace that tells the truth about your condition and then refuses to stop calling you home.
Maybe you have wandered farther than anyone knows.
Maybe you became skilled at hiding.
People see the church attendance.
Jesus sees Tuesday night.
People see the worship post.
Jesus sees the browser history.
People see the marriage photograph.
Jesus hears what happens when the door closes.
People see ministry.
Jesus sees motive.
People see generosity.
Jesus sees greed.
People hear your theology.
Jesus knows whether you actually love Him.
And somehow...
He still knocks.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Peter denied Him.
Jesus restored him.
Thomas doubted.
Jesus met him.
The thief had nothing left to offer but faith in a dying Savior beside him.
Jesus promised him paradise.
Paul carried a history of persecuting Christ's people, yet grace transformed the persecutor into a preacher of the Gospel.
The Bible is filled with people whose worst chapter looked final until God touched the page.
And maybe yours feels final too.
It isn't.
Not while Christ is calling you to repent.
Your hidden sin does not have to become your final identity.
Your compromise does not have to write the ending.
Your coldness does not have to have the last word.
Your failure does not outrank the blood of Jesus.
But grace must never become an excuse to remain where grace came to rescue you from.
Jesus does not knock so He can become another decoration in your life.
He calls you back to Himself.
Maybe this article found you while you are spiritually exhausted.
Maybe you have been pretending for months.
Maybe nobody knows how far your heart has drifted.
Then stop performing for a moment.
No polished Christian answer.
No religious mask.
Just honesty.
Do you actually want Jesus—or have you mainly wanted what Jesus can give you?
Would you still follow Him if obedience cost the relationship?
The popularity?
The secret pleasure?
The money?
The reputation?
The plan you already decided He must bless?
Would Jesus still be enough?
That question reaches deeper than emotion.
Because the opposite of lukewarm faith is not religious hype.
It is surrendered allegiance to Christ.
It is the sinner who knows he needs mercy.
The believer who still trembles at God's Word.
The wounded Christian who says, “I don't understand what You're doing, Lord, but I'm staying.”
The tempted believer who falls on his knees rather than making peace with chains.
The exhausted disciple who whispers through tears:
“Jesus, I still choose You.”
Maybe that is all you can whisper tonight.
Then whisper it.
Maybe you need to confess something.
Confess it.
Maybe you need to delete something.
Delete it.
Maybe you need to forgive.
Begin.
Maybe you need to walk away from what keeps dragging you back into darkness.
Walk.
Maybe you need another believer to pray with you.
Ask.
Maybe you have spent years pretending you belong to Christ when you have never truly trusted Him.
Come to Him.
Do not confuse conviction with rejection.
If the Word of God is exposing you, do not run from the light.
Run toward Christ.
Because the Jesus who says, “Repent,” is the same Jesus standing at the door.
The warning is not proof that mercy has disappeared.
The warning itself is mercy calling before it is too late.
And if God has been restoring you after a season of compromise, tell your testimony. Someone reading beneath this article may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores wandering people.
Do not turn the comment section into a courtroom.
Let it become a place where sinners point other sinners toward the Savior.
There may come a night when your heart starts drifting again and you need to remember what frightened you back into prayer.
Not because sharing a Christian article earns favor with God. It does not.
But if this message is faithful to Scripture and could wake someone spiritually, sharing it can become a simple act of witness.

Supporting Gospel ministry financially does not make God love you more, does not purchase blessing, and does not prove that you glorify God. Christ purchased our redemption; we cannot buy it back from Him. But voluntary generosity can glorify God when it flows from faith, love, gratitude, and a desire to help biblical truth reach others.
None of those things can substitute for opening the door.
Jesus did not die so you could become a better-looking lukewarm Christian.
He died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God, forgive those who repent and believe, make His people new, and become their Lord—not merely an accessory to an otherwise self-directed life.
before another notification steals this moment...
before conviction fades back into routine...
listen.
Perhaps the most terrifying thing about Laodicea was not that Jesus was knocking.
It was that a church bearing His name had somehow learned to live with Jesus outside the door.
Do not learn to live with the knocking.
Open the door.
Come back.
There is still grace for the ashamed.
Still mercy for the compromised.
Still forgiveness for the repentant.
Still cleansing for the stained.
Still restoration for the wanderer.
Still a cross where sinners can stop pretending.
Still an empty tomb declaring that death does not get the final sentence.
Still a Savior calling His people home.
And perhaps the warning “Do not be lukewarm” was never meant merely to scare you with the possibility that Christ might reject you.
Perhaps it was also meant to awaken you to the astonishing reality that the Christ you pushed toward the edges of your life is still standing at the door, calling you back to Himself.
The most dangerous place is not being far from Jesus and knowing it—it is being far from Jesus while believing you are close.
